title: Kiebitzr — running image vulnerabilities
description: Triage for the two questions that matter: must I patch tonight, and can I patch it at all. The first row says whether anything below is valid at all. There is deliberately no headline count of findings — see the metrics runbook on why a severity rollup per image saturates.

list.name: namespace
list.label: Namespace
list.description: Applied to kiebitzr_image_info, never to kiebitzr_vulnerability — a finding carries no namespace.

list.name: distro_types
list.label: Distribution package types
list.description: The package_type values a newer image of the same lineage is likely to carry a fix for. Everything else is compiled or bundled into the application and moves only when its publisher rebuilds.

panels.title: Is any of this valid? — read this row first
Age of last completed run
panels.description: A failed run never clears the published result, so stale findings look exactly like fresh ones. This is the only thing that says which you are looking at. Before the first successful run the metric is 0, so this reads as enormous — intended.

panels.title: Age of vulnerability database
panels.description: Runs can keep succeeding against a database that no longer knows about this week's advisories.

panels.title: Images with a risk score
panels.description: ZERO IS A RED FLAG, NOT GOOD NEWS. Grype's risk score is a product with threat as a factor, and threat is 0 without an EPSS record and without a known-exploited hit — so no series at all means the database is serving no threat data, and known_exploited reads false everywhere for want of evidence rather than for want of exploitation.

panels.title: Distinct builds running
panels.description: More than one means a rollout is in flight, or a pod is stuck on an older image. A build that predates a metric publishes nothing for it, which reads identically to a cluster with nothing to report.

panels.title: Images not examined
panels.description: Failed plus pending. These images have no findings because nobody looked, not because they are clean — and nothing in the finding metrics distinguishes the two.

panels.title: Our labels renamed by the scrape
panels.description: MUST BE 0. kiebitzr_image_info carries its own namespace and container — the pod's, which is the whole point of the metric. A Kubernetes scrape attaches labels of the same names for the Kiebitzr pod itself, and Prometheus resolves the clash by renaming ours to exported_namespace and exported_container. Every panel below then filters and groups on the exporter's own namespace instead of the workload's, which looks like an empty dashboard rather than like a misconfiguration. Fix it at the scrape with honorLabels: true (ServiceMonitor) or honor_labels: true (scrape_config) — see the running runbook.

panels.title: Which build is answering
panels.description: One row per distinct build in the deployment, matchers and workers alike.

panels.title: Must I patch tonight? — exploitation, not severity
Images exploited AND fixable
panels.description: The patch-tonight set. On a maintained cluster this is 0 for weeks at a time, which is exactly what makes it worth looking at. Trust it only when 'Images with a risk score' above is non-zero.

panels.title: Patch tonight — known-exploited with a fix available
panels.description: One row per container. The value is how many exploited-and-fixable findings its image carries.

targets.expr: count by (image_digest) (kiebitzr_vulnerability{known_exploited="true", fix_state="fixed"}) * on (image_digest) group_right () kiebitzr_image_info{namespace=~"$namespace", owner_name=~"$workload"}

panels.title: Worst single finding per container (Grype risk score)
panels.description: For ranking, not for filtering: a finding with no EPSS record scores 0, so 0 means 'no estimate' and not 'harmless'.

targets.expr: topk(10, max by (image_digest) (kiebitzr_image_risk_score) * on (image_digest) group_right () kiebitzr_image_info{namespace=~"$namespace", owner_name=~"$workload"})

panels.title: Exactly what to patch to
panels.description: The finding level behind the list on the left: which CVE, which package, the version running and the version that fixes it. Source package is what you actually fix — libssl3 and libcrypto3 are both openssl — and In file is where the artefact sits in the image, which is the only thing that says which binary carries a stdlib finding (for an apk or deb package it is just the package database). fixed_in is every fixed version the sources name, comma-separated. Read the Ecosystem column with it — for apk/deb/rpm a newer tag of the same image usually carries that version, while for a go-module or npm package the fixed version exists in a registry and may be in no published image at all. This table carries no namespace: a finding belongs to an image, so cross-reference the digest with the panel to its left.

panels.title: Exploited, but nobody has a fix — do not page on this
panels.description: Known-exploited findings whose sources state no fixed version, or state that there will not be one. There is nothing to patch to, so waking someone achieves nothing: the moves here are compensating ones — a network policy, dropping a feature or a sidecar, or retiring the workload. It is listed because an unfixable exploited vulnerability is worth knowing about, and the patch-tonight panels above deliberately exclude it.

targets.expr: count by (image_digest) (kiebitzr_vulnerability{known_exploited="true", fix_state=~"wont-fix|not-fixed|unknown"}) * on (image_digest) group_right () kiebitzr_image_info{namespace=~"$namespace", owner_name=~"$workload"}

panels.title: Is there anything to deploy? — the target tag
panels.description: Only populated with -upgrade-candidates switched on; without it this metric has no series at all. The value is how many of the digest's in-scope findings the named tag clears, and it was measured: the candidate was catalogued and matched like any other image. A row at 0 is an answer — the publisher has not shipped a fix — and is not the same as the panel to the right, where nobody could look.

panels.title: Could not be answered — not the same as no fix
panels.description: The deployability question has no answer for these digests. unorderable_builds means the repository's builds carry a fixed creation time, as reproducible builders write on purpose, so no order and therefore no negative can be derived. Treating any row here as 'no fix available' is how a page gets suppressed.

panels.title: Whose move is it? — who can get a build of this at all
The morning queue — nobody has built a fix yet, and you can ask
panels.description: Images somebody here can get a build of, where the candidate check looked and found nothing newer. That is not a dead end: it means nobody has built it yet, and the action is to ask. This list is invisible without build_access, because it sits in the same bucket as images from projects nobody can reach. It deliberately does not page — what you can do is ask, and asking is not ending (kbz:req:00001). Needs -upgrade-candidates switched on; without it neither this panel nor the next has any rows.

panels.title: Not classified yet — this axis is worth its upkeep
panels.description: Images nobody has sorted into own, reachable or none. With no -build-access-file every image is here, which is honest: it says nobody has looked, not that nothing can be done. A new workload appears here, which is the reminder to classify it. What it cannot catch is a classification that has quietly gone stale — a team dissolved, a component handed over; only a review does that.

panels.title: Can anybody get a build of what we run?
panels.description: The fleet by build access. A large unknown slice is not a verdict about the images — it is the state of the classification file, and the one number this axis has to be read against.

panels.title: Your move — what bumping the image tag clears
Distribution packages with a fix, per workload
panels.description: High and Critical findings in apk/deb/rpm packages. The base image's maintainer tracks the distribution's advisories, so a newer tag of the same lineage usually carries the fix. Aggregated with max, not sum: two containers of one workload sharing a digest would otherwise count the same image twice.

targets.expr: max by (namespace, owner_kind, owner_name, image) (count by (image_digest) (kiebitzr_vulnerability{severity=~"High|Critical", fix_state="fixed", package_type=~"$distro_types"}) * on (image_digest) group_right () kiebitzr_image_info{namespace=~"$namespace", owner_name=~"$workload"})

panels.title: Root causes, not findings
panels.description: A handful of source packages usually explains most of the count. Grouped by source_package, so one advisory against openssl counts once rather than once per binary package built from it (libssl3, libcrypto3). One artefact survives that: Syft catalogues compiled Python bytecode under several names, which triple-counts one thing — an ignore rule is the answer there, and what it hides is counted in the blind-spots row.

panels.title: Not your move — waiting on whoever publishes the image
Compiled or bundled into the application, per workload
panels.description: Go modules, npm, python, java archives. fix_state says a fixed VERSION exists; it does not say the fix can reach this container. Nothing is patched inside a running container, and for these a newer tag of the same image usually does not help either — only a rebuild by the publisher does. This list belongs in a vendor conversation, not in your maintenance window. Read it with the row above: for an image your own team builds, or one a team you can ask builds, this is not 'not your move' at all — the remedy is a rebuild somebody here can trigger. It is for build_access="none" that this list is a vendor ticket.

targets.expr: max by (namespace, owner_kind, owner_name, image) (count by (image_digest) (kiebitzr_vulnerability{severity=~"High|Critical", fix_state="fixed", package_type!~"$distro_types"}) * on (image_digest) group_right () kiebitzr_image_info{namespace=~"$namespace", owner_name=~"$workload"})

panels.title: Share not actionable here
panels.description: Of all fixable High and Critical findings, the fraction that only the image's publisher can resolve. On the pilot cluster this was 47 % — half of what the metrics called 'fixed' was out of the cluster operator's hands.

panels.title: Blind spots — what this dashboard cannot see
Images the last run could not analyse
panels.description: The reason is the stage it failed at, not the registry's message — that is in the 'image failed' log line beside the digest. unreachable_image is usually a missing registry credential, a wrong -platform, or an image that only exists in a node's local store.

panels.title: Not catalogued yet when the run published
panels.description: Pending is not failed and it is not clean: cataloguing ran out of its budget before reaching these. Expected on a cold start and it has to fall away; still pending after days means the catalogue budget or the worker pool is too small.

panels.title: No findings — clean, or unexamined?
panels.description: Containers whose image produced no findings at all. Cross-check every row against the two panels to the left: what appears there is unexamined, not clean. And an excluded namespace appears in neither — it is invisible to this dashboard entirely.

panels.title: Hidden by a filter — on purpose
panels.description: The one blind spot this service creates itself: -min-severity, -only-fixed and an ignore rule all remove findings, and this is how many. Watch the jump, not the level — a steady count is the configuration working, a tripling overnight is new findings being hidden. The reasons are disjoint, so they can be summed. No rows means the last run removed nothing, which also covers no filter being configured; an excluded namespace appears nowhere at all, because it is dropped before any image of it is read.

panels.title: Drift and throughput
Same tag, different digests — a re-pull may be the whole fix
panels.description: One tag running at two digests: with imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent a node that already holds the image never pulls it again, so a tag that moved reached some nodes and not others. On the pilot cluster the stale digest carried 141 findings more, including an already-fixed openssl High — cleared by re-pulling the same tag, with nothing to upgrade. Which digest is behind is not in the metrics; compare the findings per digest with the query in the metrics runbook. A rollout in flight looks the same and clears itself, so what counts is drift that survives the next run.

targets.expr: count by (image, image_digest) (kiebitzr_image_info) and on (image) (count by (image) (count by (image, image_digest) (kiebitzr_image_info)) > 1)

renameByName.image: Tag as the pod asked for it

sort.field: Tag as the pod asked for it

panels.title: Findings over time
panels.description: Four buckets, not six: an ordered scale gets one hue light to dark, never a set of unrelated colours, and Medium and below are not a work list. Watch the shape, not the absolute number — a step change is a new advisory batch or a new image, a slope is drift.

panels.title: Cataloguing work outstanding
panels.description: Only exists with a worker pool. Stays high through a run means more workers would help — scale on this and not on worker CPU, because a worker spends its time waiting on a registry.

panels.title: Worker throughput
panels.description: What the pool is actually getting through, per hour. A separate panel on purpose: two measures of different scale never share one axis.
